question: A patient with cancer pain on morphine 30 mg/day requires 60 mg/day after 3 months to achieve the same analgesia. She has no drug-seeking behaviour, takes all doses as prescribed, and functions normally. This presentation BEST represents:

answers.text: Addiction — characterised by compulsive use and loss of control over drug-taking

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Addiction requires compulsive use, craving, and continued use despite harm. This patient uses the drug as prescribed for a legitimate indication with no loss of control — addiction criteria are not met.

answers.text: Physical dependence — requiring the drug to prevent withdrawal symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Physical dependence is likely present (she would experience withdrawal if opioids were stopped abruptly), but that is not what the scenario is primarily describing. The scenario explicitly describes a rising dose requirement for the same effect — that is tolerance.

answers.text: Pharmacological tolerance — requiring higher doses to achieve the same analgesic effect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tolerance is the pharmacological adaptation producing reduced effect at a given dose (or the need for higher doses to achieve the same effect). It occurs predictably with opioids via receptor downregulation. Importantly, tolerance is not addiction — this patient has no aberrant drug-seeking behaviour.

answers.text: Pseudoaddiction — drug-seeking behaviour driven by under-treatment of pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pseudoaddiction occurs when patients appear drug-seeking because their pain is under-treated. This patient does not display drug-seeking behaviour — she is on an adequate regimen that has simply lost potency over time due to tolerance.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key finding is dose escalation to maintain the same analgesic effect — this is the definition of pharmacological tolerance. Distinguish it from physical dependence (withdrawal-driven) and addiction (compulsive, harm-ignoring use).

Correct. Tolerance = reduced effect at the same dose. Physical dependence = withdrawal on abrupt discontinuation. Addiction = compulsive use despite harm. These three are distinct and must not be conflated — particularly for cancer pain management.
